paragraphs: The argument was over. But strangely, Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had been so cheerful, suddenly began to scowl. He scowled and gulped down brandy, and it was already one glass too many.

“Off with you, Jesuits!” he shouted at the servants. “Go away, Smerdyakov. I’ll send you the gold piece I promised you today, but get out! Don’t cry, Grigory. Go to Marfa. She’ll comfort you and put you to bed. The rascals won’t even let us sit in peace after dinner,” he snapped peevishly, as the servants withdrew at once at his word.
“Smerdyakov pokes his nose in every night after dinner now. It’s you he’s so interested in. What have you done to fascinate him?” he added, to Ivan.
“Nothing at all,” answered Ivan. “He likes having a high opinion of me. He’s a lackey and a mean soul. Raw material for a revolution, though, when the time comes.”
“For a revolution?”
“There will be others, and better ones. But there will be some like him too. His kind will come first, and the better ones after.”
“And when will the time come?”
“The rocket will go off and fizzle out, maybe. So far the peasants don’t much like listening to these soup-makers.”
“Ah, brother, but a Balaam’s ass like that thinks and thinks, and the devil knows where he ends up.”
“He’s storing up ideas,” said Ivan, smiling.

“You see, I know he can’t stand me, or anyone else, even you, though you imagine he has a high opinion of you. It’s worse with Alyosha: he despises Alyosha. But he doesn’t steal, that’s one thing, and he’s no gossip. He keeps his mouth shut and doesn’t air our dirty linen in public. He makes excellent fish pasties too. But, damn him, is he worth talking about so much?”
“Of course he isn’t.”

“And as for the ideas he may be hatching, the Russian peasant, generally speaking, needs a thrashing. I’ve always said so. Our peasants are swindlers and don’t deserve pity, and it’s a good thing they still get flogged now and then. Russia is rich in birches. If they cut down the forests, it would be the ruin of Russia. I stand up for the clever people. We’ve stopped thrashing the peasants, we’ve grown so clever, but they go on thrashing themselves. And a good thing too. ‘For with what measure ye mete it shall be measured to you again,’ or how does it go? Anyhow, it will be measured. But Russia is all swinishness. My dear boy, if you only knew how I hate Russia.... That is, not Russia, but all this vice! But maybe I do mean Russia. _Tout cela c’est de la cochonnerie_.... Do you know what I like? I like wit.”
“You’ve had another glass. That’s enough.”

“Wait a bit. I’ll have one more, and then another, and then I’ll stop. No, hold on, you interrupted me. At Mokroe I was talking to an old man, and he told me: ‘There’s nothing we like so much as sentencing girls to be thrashed, and we always give the lads the job of thrashing them. And the girl he thrashes today, the young man will ask to marry tomorrow. So it suits the girls too,’ he said. There’s a set of de Sades for you! But it’s clever, anyway. Shall we go over and have a look at it, eh? Alyosha, are you blushing? Don’t be shy, child. I’m sorry I didn’t stay to dinner at the Superior’s and tell the monks about the girls at Mokroe. Alyosha, don’t be angry that I insulted your Superior this morning. I lost my temper. If there is a God, if He exists, then of course I’m to blame, and I’ll have to answer for it. But if there’s no God at all, what do they deserve, your fathers? It’s not enough to cut their heads off, because they hold back progress. Would you believe it, Ivan, that this lacerates my feelings? No, you don’t believe it, I can see from your eyes. You believe what people say, that I’m nothing but a buffoon. Alyosha, do you believe I’m nothing but a buffoon?”
“No, I don’t believe it.”

“And I believe you don’t, and that you’re telling the truth. You look sincere and you speak sincerely. But not Ivan. Ivan’s superior.... I’d make an end of your monks all the same. I’d take all that mystic stuff and wipe it out, once and for all, all over Russia, to bring every fool to his senses. And think of the gold and silver that would flow into the mint!”
“But why wipe it out?” asked Ivan.
“So that Truth may prevail. That’s why.”
“Well, if Truth were to prevail, you know, you’d be the first to be robbed and wiped out.”

“Ah! You’re probably right. Ah, what an ass I am!” burst out Fyodor Pavlovitch, striking himself lightly on the forehead. “Well, then, your monastery can stand, Alyosha, if that’s how it is. And we clever people will sit snug and enjoy our brandy. You know, Ivan, it must have been ordained like that by the Almighty Himself. Ivan, speak, is there a God or not? Wait, speak the truth, speak seriously. Why are you laughing again?”
“I’m laughing because you made a clever remark just now about Smerdyakov’s belief in the two saints who could move mountains.”
“Why, am I like him now, then?”
“Very much.”

“Well, that shows I’m a Russian too, and I have a Russian characteristic. And you can be caught in the same way, though you are a philosopher. Shall I catch you? What do you bet that I’ll catch you tomorrow? Speak, all the same, is there a God or not? Only be serious. I want you to be serious now.”
“No, there is no God.”
“Alyosha, is there a God?”
“There is.”
“Ivan, and is there immortality of some sort, just a little, just a tiny bit?”
“There is no immortality either.”
“None at all?”
“None at all.”
“So there’s absolute nothingness. Perhaps there’s just something? Anything is better than nothing!”
“Absolute nothingness.”
“Alyosha, is there immortality?”
“There is.”
“God and immortality?”
“God and immortality. In God is immortality.”

“H’m! It’s more likely that Ivan’s right. Good Lord! To think what faith, what force of every kind, man has wasted for nothing on that dream, and for how many thousands of years. Who is it that’s laughing at man? Ivan! For the last time, once and for all, is there a God or not? I’m asking for the last time!”
“And for the last time, there is not.”
“Who is laughing at mankind, Ivan?”
“It must be the devil,” said Ivan, smiling.
“And the devil? Does he exist?”
“No, there’s no devil either.”
“What a pity. Damn it all, what wouldn’t I do to the man who first invented God! Hanging him from a bitter aspen tree would be too good for him.”
“There would have been no civilization if they hadn’t invented God.”
“There wouldn’t? Without God?”
“No. And there would have been no brandy either. But I’m going to take your brandy away from you, all the same.”
“Stop, stop, stop, dear boy, one more little glass. I’ve hurt Alyosha’s feelings. You’re not angry with me, Alyosha? My dear little Alexey!”
“No, I’m not angry. I know your thoughts. Your heart is better than your head.”
“My heart better than my head, is it? Oh, Lord! And that from you. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?”
“Yes.”

“You must love him” (Fyodor Pavlovitch was by this time very drunk). “Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. But I was worked up. Still, there’s wit in that elder, don’t you think, Ivan?”
“Very likely.”

“There is, there is. _Il y a du Piron là-dedans._ He’s a Jesuit, a Russian one, that is. Since he’s an honorable man, there’s a hidden indignation boiling inside him at having to pretend and put on holiness.”
“But of course he believes in God.”

“Not a bit of it. Didn’t you know? Why, he tells everyone so himself. That is, not everyone, but all the clever people who come to him. He said straight out to Governor Schultz not long ago: ‘_Credo_, but I don’t know in what.’”
“Really?”

“He really did. But I respect him. There’s something of Mephistopheles about him, or rather of ‘The Hero of Our Time’ ... Arbenin, or whatever his name is?... You see, he’s a sensualist. He’s such a sensualist that I’d be afraid for my daughter or my wife if she went to confess to him. You know, when he starts telling stories.... The year before last he invited us to tea, tea with liqueur (the ladies send him liqueur), and began telling us about the old days till we nearly split our sides.... Especially how he once cured a paralyzed woman. ‘If my legs weren’t bad, I know a dance I could dance for you,’ he said. What do you say to that? ‘I’ve played plenty of tricks in my time,’ said he. He did Dernidov, the merchant, out of sixty thousand.”
“What, he stole it?”

“The merchant brought him the money, as to a man he could trust, saying, ‘Keep it for me, friend, the police will search my place tomorrow.’ And he kept it. ‘You gave it to the Church,’ he declared. I said to him: ‘You’re a scoundrel,’ I said. ‘No,’ said he, ‘I’m not a scoundrel, I’m broad-minded.’ But that wasn’t him, that was somebody else. I’ve mixed him up with somebody else ... without noticing it. Come, another glass and that’s enough. Take the bottle away, Ivan. I’ve been telling lies. Why didn’t you stop me, Ivan, and tell me I was lying?”
“I knew you’d stop on your own.”
“That’s a lie. You did it out of spite, plain spite against me. You despise me. You came to me and despised me in my own house.”
“Well, I’m leaving. You’ve had too much brandy.”
“I’ve begged you for Christ’s sake to go to Tchermashnya for a day or two, and you won’t go.”
“I’ll go tomorrow if you’re so set on it.”
“You won’t go. You want to keep an eye on me. That’s what you want, you spiteful fellow. That’s why you won’t go.”
The old man kept it up. He had reached that stage of drunkenness when a drunkard who has been harmless till then tries to pick a quarrel and assert himself.

“Why are you looking at me? Why do you look like that? Your eyes look at me and say, ‘You ugly drunk!’ Your eyes are suspicious. They’re contemptuous.... You’ve come here with some scheme. Alyosha, now, looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn’t despise me. Alexey, you mustn’t love Ivan.”
“Don’t be ill-tempered with my brother. Stop attacking him,” Alyosha said firmly.
“Oh, all right. Ugh, my head aches. Take away the brandy, Ivan. It’s the third time I’ve told you.”
He brooded for a moment, and then a slow, cunning grin spread over his face.

“Don’t be angry with a feeble old man, Ivan. I know you don’t love me, but don’t be angry all the same. You’ve nothing to love me for. You go to Tchermashnya. I’ll come to you myself and bring you a present. I’ll show you a little wench there. I’ve had my eye on her a long time. She’s still running around barefoot. Don’t be afraid of barefoot wenches—don’t despise them—they’re pearls!”
And he kissed his hand with a smack.

“To my thinking,” he revived at once, seeming to sober up the instant he touched on his favorite topic. “To my thinking ... Ah, you boys! You children, you little sucking-pigs, to my thinking ... I never thought a woman ugly in my life—that’s been my rule! Can you understand that? How could you understand it? You’ve got milk in your veins, not blood. You’re not out of your shells yet. My rule has been that in every woman you can find something devilishly interesting that you wouldn’t find in any other. Only you have to know how to find it, that’s the point! That’s a talent! To my mind there are no ugly women. The very fact that she’s a woman is half the battle ... but how could you understand that? Even in _vieilles filles_, even in them you can discover something that makes you simply wonder that men have been such fools as to let them grow old without noticing them. Barefoot girls or plain ones, you have to take by surprise. Didn’t you know that? You have to astound them till they’re fascinated, shaken, ashamed that such a gentleman should fall in love with such a little slut. It’s a jolly good thing that there always are and always will be masters and slaves in the world, so there will always be a little maid-of-all-work and her master, and you know, that’s all that’s needed for happiness. Wait ... listen, Alyosha, I always used to surprise your mother, but in a different way. I paid no attention to her at all, but all at once, when the moment came, I’d be all devotion to her, crawl on my knees, kiss her feet, and I always, always—I remember it as if it were today—brought her to that tinkling, quiet, nervous, queer little laugh. It was peculiar to her. I knew her attacks always used to begin like that. The next day she would start shrieking hysterically, and this little laugh was not a sign of delight, though it made a very good counterfeit. That’s the great thing, to know how to handle everyone. Once Belyavsky—he was a handsome fellow, and rich—used to like to come here and hang about her—suddenly gave me a slap in the face in her presence. And she—such a mild sheep—why, I thought she would knock me down for that blow. How she flew at me! ‘You’re beaten, beaten now,’ she said. ‘You took a blow from him. You’ve been trying to sell me to him,’ she said.... ‘And how dared he strike you in front of me! Don’t dare come near me again, never, never! Run at once, challenge him to a duel!’... Then I took her to the monastery to bring her to her senses. The holy Fathers prayed her back to reason. But I swear to God, Alyosha, I never insulted the poor crazy girl! Only once, perhaps, in the first year; she was very fond of praying then. She used to keep the feasts of Our Lady especially, and used to throw me out of her room on those days. I’ll knock that mysticism out of her, thought I! ‘Here,’ said I, ‘you see your holy image. Here it is. Here I take it down. You believe it’s miraculous, but watch, I’ll spit on it right now and nothing will happen to me for it!’... When she saw it, good Lord! I thought she would kill me. But she only jumped up, wrung her hands, then suddenly hid her face in them, began trembling all over and fell on the floor ... fell all in a heap. Alyosha, Alyosha, what’s the matter?”

The old man jumped up in alarm. From the moment he began speaking about Alyosha’s mother, a change had gradually come over Alyosha’s face. He flushed crimson, his eyes glowed, his lips quivered. The old sot had gone on spluttering, noticing nothing, until something very strange happened to Alyosha. Exactly what he was describing in the crazy woman was suddenly repeated in Alyosha. He jumped up from his seat just as his mother was said to have done, wrung his hands, hid his face in them, and fell back in his chair, shaking all over in a hysterical fit of sudden, violent, silent weeping. His extraordinary resemblance to his mother struck the old man particularly.

“Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! It’s like her, exactly as she used to be then, his mother. Spray some water on him from your mouth, that’s what I used to do to her. He’s upset about his mother, his mother,” he muttered to Ivan.

“But she was my mother too, I believe, his mother. Wasn’t she?” said Ivan, with uncontrolled anger and contempt. The old man shrank before his flashing eyes. But something very strange had happened, though only for a second: it really seemed to have slipped the old man’s mind that Alyosha’s mother actually was Ivan’s mother too.

“Your mother?” he muttered, not understanding. “What do you mean? What mother are you talking about? Was she?... Why, damn it! Of course she was yours too! Damn it! My mind has never been so clouded before. Excuse me, why, I was thinking, Ivan.... He he he!” He stopped. A broad, drunken, half-senseless grin spread over his face.
At that moment a terrible noise and clamor was heard in the hall, there were violent shouts, the door was flung open, and Dmitri burst into the room. The old man ran to Ivan in terror.
“He’ll kill me! He’ll kill me! Don’t let him get at me!” he screamed, clinging to the skirt of Ivan’s coat.
